Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The notes are a mix of observations, player comments, and tentative ideas; distinguish among those categories rather than presenting every suggestion as a decision. Do not add rules, outcomes, or explanations that are not in the notes. Use the numbered sections below as source material, not as a required order for the final summary.

1. Session and table

The playtest took place on Saturday afternoon at Mara’s apartment, with four players: Mara, who designed the game; Dev; Lin; and Owen. They played one full game and stopped after the final harbor phase, then spent about twenty minutes talking through the session. The game uses a shared map of a fictional coastal town. Players move small boats between docks, collect cargo, and complete delivery cards before the storm marker reaches the end of its track. The prototype was made from a printed map, index-card cargo pieces, colored cubes, and a paper storm track. Mara had changed the cargo limit since the previous test, but none of the other rules had changed. The group had played a short introductory round together the week before, so the players recognized the basic movement and delivery rules.

2. Opening turns and route choices

The first two rounds were quiet. Dev and Owen moved toward the eastern docks, while Lin stayed near the central market and picked up two small cargo pieces. Mara said the western route was “short on paper, but it keeps getting crowded.” On the third round, Dev’s boat and Owen’s boat both tried to enter Pier 4. The current rule lets the first boat remain there and makes the second boat move to the nearest open dock. Owen moved to Pier 3 without a dispute, but asked whether players could agree to share a dock. Mara said that they could not under the current rules and wrote the question in the margin of her notebook. Lin later said the automatic move felt easy to resolve, though she had not yet tried a route that ended with no nearby open dock.

3. Cargo and delivery decisions

The new cargo limit was two pieces per boat. Lin remembered the change, but Dev initially loaded a third piece at the market. Mara caught it before Dev moved; he removed one piece and continued. Dev said, “I forgot we’d tightened the limit,” and did not suggest that the written rule was unclear. During the middle rounds, Owen carried one large cargo piece and passed on two small deliveries because his boat was already full. Lin completed a delivery at the lighthouse and received the printed reward of one coin. Mara and Dev each completed a market delivery. The notes do not record the exact coin totals after each delivery. Near the end, Owen asked whether a player could unload cargo at a dock without completing a delivery card. Mara checked the cards and said the prototype did not describe that action. Owen kept the cargo aboard, and the group left the question unresolved.

4. Storm track and pace

The storm marker advanced at the end of each round. It reached the final space after round eight, which triggered the harbor phase as written on the reference sheet. Players had expected the game to last around seven rounds, based on the introductory play, but nobody said the longer game felt frustrating. Dev called the final approach “tense in a good way,” while Lin said she wanted one more turn to finish a delivery. The notes do not say whether an extra turn would have changed the winner or any player’s score. Mara noted that two of the storm spaces have small wave icons, but the group did not use those icons during this session because their effect is not included in the current rules sheet. No one treated the icons as an active rule during play.

5. Player comments and observed friction

Players consulted the reference sheet three times: once to check the cargo limit, once to confirm the storm trigger, and once to check the reward for a lighthouse delivery. Dev said the cargo limit might be easier to notice if it appeared beside the boat illustration as well as in the setup text. This was a suggestion, not a change made during the session. Lin liked the shared map and said other players’ routes made her reconsider where to go. Owen said he understood why his boat had been moved from Pier 4, but found it hard to compare the nearest open dock options quickly. Mara observed that the map’s dock labels were readable in daylight, though the small print became difficult to see when players leaned back from the table. Nobody reported confusion about how to move a boat between connected docks.

6. End of game and discussion

At the end of the harbor phase, the group counted the coins and delivery marks using the prototype’s scoring sheet. Mara had the highest total, Lin was second, Dev was third, and Owen was fourth. The notes include no exact final scores. Owen said he had enjoyed planning routes, even when the busy docks forced him to change direction. Lin said the ending felt close, but the notes do not record the score gap. Dev asked whether completed delivery cards should be discarded or kept beside each player; the prototype currently tells players to keep them, and the question concerned the visual arrangement rather than an unclear written rule. Mara did not announce a winner’s reward or any change to the scoring system.

7. Follow-up ideas recorded by Mara

Mara wrote down four possible revisions for later consideration: add the cargo limit beside the boat illustration; test a rule that allows two boats to share a dock; make the wave icons’ status clearer on the map or rule sheet; and try a slightly larger print size for the dock labels. These are untested ideas, not decisions or confirmed changes. The notes do not say when another playtest will happen, whether the same players will attend, or which idea Mara plans to try first.

Please turn these notes into a concise, readable summary of about 350 to 500 words. Use a short title and organize the summary with numbered sections. Cover the session setup, notable play patterns, player feedback, ending, and open questions without repeating every turn in sequence. Retain the quoted comments exactly as written if you include them, and attribute comments to the named speaker. Make clear when a point is an observation, a player suggestion, or an unresolved question. Do not infer exact scores, explain the wave icons, settle the dock-sharing or unloading questions, or describe any tentative revision as adopted. ## 1. Game and rules draft
Lantern Ferry is for two to four players. It is cooperative: everyone works together to get three supply crates from the north bank to South Wharf before the storm marker reaches space 8. The printed board is a 7-by-7 river map with a north bank, a south bank, five marked landing spaces, and three route tiles. The storm track has spaces 0 through 8 and starts at 0. The players share one ferry pawn, which can carry two crates at once.

The draft rules say each player gets two actions on their turn. The listed choices are to move the ferry by playing a route card, load one crate, or repair a damaged landing. There are 30 weather cards, 12 event cards, and a four-page printed rules draft. The box has six wooden crates, although the goal requires three. Do not fill in unspecified rules, including what happens when a deck runs out or when a damaged landing is used.

## 2. Session setting and available materials
The table seats four, and the 90-minute session must include setup and the conversation afterward. The community room has decent light and a wall clock, but no projector. I can bring my phone and use its timer. I do not want to record audio or video.

Available materials are the board printout, ferry pawn, four player pawns, six crates, route tiles, both decks, the draft rules, pencils, sticky notes, and one notebook. There is only one copy of the rules, so each player cannot have a copy. I can bring scrap paper if a quick private worksheet would help, but I have not made one. Nothing is laminated, and I do not plan to make replacement components before Sunday. Describe what to put on the table and a sensible arrangement using only these materials; do not invent components.

## 3. Previous observations and points of interest
In an earlier two-person kitchen-table tryout, the players stopped twice to look up what counts as a landing, and one person forgot to move the storm marker after drawing weather. That was not the four-person session described here; do not treat it as evidence of how this session will go.

Jo said, “The ferry can carry two crates, but I keep thinking it can take three.” In the new draft, the capacity is printed beside the ferry picture, but I do not know whether the wording fixes the confusion. The draft also uses the phrase “repair a damaged landing” without a picture. I am curious whether first-time players understand both points. Do not have the facilitator draw attention to them at the start or otherwise plant those ideas.

## 4. Requested playtest sequence
Cover the full sequence: the day-before check; arrival and setup; welcoming the group; explaining the session; starting the game; observing; stopping; debriefing; and packing up. Plan for one complete attempt if the group can finish within the available time. Do not suggest squeezing in a second game.

Explain how I can introduce the goal and basic process while giving players time to read the draft themselves. Players may ask me questions, and I may answer if they are stuck, but I do not want to narrate every decision or immediately rescue them from ordinary uncertainty. Distinguish an unclear rule question from ordinary strategic discussion rather than treating all table talk as a problem.

## 5. Observation and timing
Suggest a light way to take notes in the notebook or on sticky notes; this is not a formal study. I especially want to notice when someone rereads the rules, asks what a term means, forgets a step, disagrees about a rule, or seems unable to take a turn. Also include moments when one player explains something to another and when the group moves on without my help. Do not assume that a pause means confusion, and do not diagnose why someone acted as they did.

I need to participate enough to keep the session moving while still remembering what happened without writing constantly. Include a realistic rough time plan for the 90 minutes and some flexibility if the game is still underway near the end.

## 6. Debrief and close
Include a few neutral post-play questions for all four players, with room for their own observations. Ask about the two areas noted above without telling them what answers I expect. Ask about the rules draft and component visibility, not whether they liked me as facilitator. Explain how to end on time if the group has not finished, without calling an unfinished attempt a win or a loss. Include a brief reminder to thank the players, collect the pieces, and keep observed events separate from my guesses in the notes.

Return a usable prompt requesting step-by-step playtest instructions.
